title: Bless before taking (Berakhot 35a–b)
hookLine: enjoying the world without a blessing is like taking what is holy; "The earth is the LORD's"
tomorrow: what does the soul enjoy that the body doesn't?

cards: At a friend's house, opening their fridge without asking feels wrong, even if they'd say yes. So is eating an apple without a word a kind of taking? The Talmud says, more or less, yes.
To enjoy anything of this world without a blessing is like making personal use of something holy, something that belongs to the Temple.

teach.b: Then Rabbi Levi finds two verses that seem to fight. One psalm says: "The earth is the LORD's, and the fulness thereof." Another says: "the earth hath he given to the children of men."
Which is it, God's or ours? His answer: both, in order.
Before the blessing, the earth is the LORD's. After the blessing, it's given to us. The blessing is the asking, the moment the gift changes hands.
That's why Jews say a short blessing before eating, a different one for bread, for fruit of the tree, for what grows from the ground. Here's a neighbor who knows this table.
Noa's friend Owen grew up Lutheran, and his family says grace before dinner.

Christians read in the New Testament, in Paul's first letter to Timothy, that what God made is good, "and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving," because it is made holy "by the word of God and prayer."

teach.h: ONE GRACE, OR A BLESSING PER FOOD.
teach.b: Words before food, and food received as a gift: that's shared, in each tradition's own voice. And one honest difference.
The Talmud puts it as taking: without the blessing, it's still the LORD's. The letter starts from good: it's good already, received with thanks.
And where Owen's family says one grace for the meal, a Jewish table often blesses each kind of food by name.

how: Jews say a short blessing (bracha) before eating, with different blessings for bread, wine, fruit of the tree, what grows from the ground and other foods; the Talmud on Berakhot 35a–b gives the reason.

o: only eat food that has been blessed by a rabbi first
give part of every meal away before you eat the rest
say a blessing first, so what's God's is given to you

games.q: two verses, one answer — tap the pairs.
p: given to the children of men
like using what's holy for yourself
one grace for the whole meal

s: the two psalms contradict each other, so one must be wrong
Rabbi Levi: one is before the blessing, the other after.
a Christian letter also says food is made holy by prayer
1 Timothy 4: received with thanksgiving, made holy by the word of God and prayer.
Jewish and Christian meal blessings work exactly the same way
both give thanks before food; the Talmud frames it as asking for what's God's, and often blesses each kind of food.

games.q: a coworker offers you the first slice of a birthday cake she baked. you're starving. what does Rabbi Levi's reading suggest about that first bite?
o: eat right away; it's yours the second she hands it over.
pause and thank first: the thanks is what makes the gift change hands.
turn it down; taking something someone else made is a kind of theft.
games.why: before the blessing, the earth is the LORD's; after it, given to us. the asking is the handoff, not a refusal.

practice: Hold something to eat or drink, and before the first taste, stop. If you know a blessing for it, say it; if not, just name where it came from. Then taste slowly, and notice that it's been handed to you.

wordCard.voice: Bless before taking. Before the blessing the earth is the LORD's; after it, the earth is given to the children of men.

orig.note: Hebrew: blessing; the tractate Berakhot is named for blessings.

carryVoice: Something for the table: bless before taking, and the gift changes hands. Thirty-one of fifty down.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 35a–b (enjoying this world without a blessing is like misusing consecrated things; Rabbi Levi: Psalm 24:1 before the blessing, Psalm 115:16 after)
